You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 0.76 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal (weak); Ip = 12 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 12 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 6800 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 22000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weakest excitation; Ip = 8 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 22000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 10 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 12 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       0.56   0.566    11.6       -    0.0314  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S2      0.558   0.563    11.2       -    0.0457  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       2.24    2.26    35.4   0.329     0.228  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S4      0.334   0.339    8.95       -   0.00508  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S5      0.573   0.581    15.7       -    0.0329  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S6      0.459   0.462     6.1       -    0.0211  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 4 of 12.

RESULTS OF YOUR PREVIOUS ROUND:

Design 1 'Single-Sync-Boost': failed the screen and was not tuned (topology 42bbd2d86bfe).
L1 L pzp n1 0.002

what this means:
- with the output fixed at 1.8 V, the net power delivered covers only -189 % of the load's need on S2 (heavy load), -618 % of the load's need on S4 (weakest excitation), -286 % of the load's need on S6 (Cp +20 %, hot) (best of the value presets tried)

REPEATED PROBLEM: your last three designs all show the same failure: too little power reaches the output on some conditions [underpower]. Change the part of the circuit responsible for it rather than its values.

BEST DESIGNS SO FAR (values already tuned):

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Power a sensor load $R_L$ from a piezo transducer.
    *   Target $V_{out}$: $1.8\text{ V}$ to $3.6\text{ V}$.
    *   Ripple: $\le 0.05\text{ V}$.
    *   Startup: $\le 0.4\text{ s}$.
    *   Conditions: $S1$ to $S6$.
    *   Piezo: Sinusoidal current source, $C_p = 25\text{ nF}$, $R_{leak} = 20\text{ M}\Omega$, $V_{oc,peak} \approx 0.76\text{ V}$ (for $S1$).
    *   Constraint: $V_{oc,peak}$ is *very low* ($0.76\text{ V}$), whereas the target $V_{out}$ is $1.8\text{ V}$. This means a passive rectifier (FBR) will never work because the diode drops ($\sim 0.25\text{ V}$ for DSCH) and the peak voltage are too low to push charge into a $1.8\text{ V}$ capacitor.

    *   The piezo source is effectively a voltage source $V_{piezo}(t) = \frac{I_p}{2\pi f C_p} \sin(2\pi f t)$.
    *   Peak voltage $\approx 0.76\text{ V}$.
    *   Since $V_{oc,peak} < 1.8\text{ V}$, we *must* use a DC-DC boost converter or a switching-based energy harvester (like SSHI - Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor).
    *   Standard SSHI usually works by flipping the voltage across $C_p$ to increase the available energy per cycle. However, the target $V_{out}$ is higher than the open-circuit voltage of the piezo.

    *   FBR: Failed (too low voltage).
    *   P-SSHI (Design [c0034]): Failed. The screening showed it *could* deliver power (2364% etc.), but in simulation, $V_{out}$ never rose. This suggests the "startup" phase is impossible because the circuit cannot kick-start itself from $0\text{ V}$ or the diode bridge prevents the SSHI mechanism from working effectively during the startup transition.
    *   Single-Sync-Boost: Failed screen (negative power). The topology was likely wrong.

    *   The core problem is the extremely low $V_{oc}$ of the piezo ($0.76\text{ V}$).
    *   We need a way to boost this voltage.
    *   A typical SSHI circuit uses a switch to invert the voltage on $C_p$, effectively increasing the voltage swing. To get charge *out* to a $1.8\text{ V}$ rail, the peak voltage on $C_p$ must exceed $1.8\text{ V} + V_{diode}$.
    *   Standard SSHI:
        1.  Piezo charges $C_p$.
        2.  At peak, a switch closes $L$ across $C_p$ for a short time, inverting $V_{Cp}$.
        3.  Charge is then pushed through a rectifier to $C_{out}$.
    *   However, if $V_{oc}$ is $0.76\text{ V}$, the voltage on $C_p$ without SSHI only reaches $0.76\text{ V}$. With SSHI, it can reach $2 \times V_{oc} \approx 1.52\text{ V}$. Still below $1.8\text{ V}$.
    *   Wait, let's re-read the piezo model. $I_p = 12\text{ uA}$ peak. $f = 100\text{ Hz}$. $C_p = 25\text{ nF}$.
        $V_{oc} = \frac{I_p}{2\pi f C_p} = \frac{12\text{e-6}}{2\pi \cdot 100 \cdot 25\text{e-9}} = \frac{12\text{e-6}}{1.57\text{e-5}} \approx 0.76\text{ V}$. Correct.

    *   If $V_{oc} = 0.76\text{ V}$, a passive bridge is useless. An SSHI circuit increases the voltage on $C_p$. The theoretical limit of voltage on $C_p$ for a perfectly synchronized switch is $V_{max} = \frac{2 I_p}{2\pi f C_p} \approx 1.52\text{ V}$. This is still not enough to reach $1.8\text{ V}$.
    *   Is there another way? A Boost converter.
        A boost converter requires a switch and an inductor.
        Topology: Piezo $\rightarrow$ Inductor $\rightarrow$ Switch to GND $\rightarrow$ Diode $\rightarrow$ Output.
        But the piezo is a current source in parallel with $C_p$.
        If we treat the piezo as a source, we can use a synchronous boost.
        $V_{out} = V_{in} \cdot \frac{1}{1-D}$.
        But $V_{in}$ here is the piezo voltage.

    *   Let's try a different approach: **Synchronous Charge Extraction (SCE)** or a variation of **SSHI**.
    *   Since the goal is $1.8\text{ V}$ and $V_{oc}$ is $0.76\text{ V}$, we absolutely need an inductive boost.
    *   Let's look at the "Single-Sync-Boost" that failed. It had two inductors. Let's try a simpler boost.
    *   Piezo terminals: $pzp, pzn$.
    *   Let's use one of the terminals as ground ($pzn = 0$).
    *   $pzp \rightarrow L1 \rightarrow$ (node $n1$).
    *   (node $n1$) $\rightarrow$ switch $S1$ $\rightarrow 0$.
    *   (node $n1$) $\rightarrow$ diode $D1$ $\rightarrow out$.
    *   When $S1$ is closed, $L1$ charges from the piezo. When $S1$ opens, $L1$ dumps charge into $out$.
    *   Since the piezo is a current source $I_p \sin(\omega t)$, we should close the switch when the current is flowing *into* the inductor.

    *   Actually, the piezo is $I_p \sin(\omega t)$ in parallel with $C_p$.
    *   Let's try a **Parallel-SSHI** (P-SSHI) again, but make sure the rectification is efficient. The previous P-SSHI failed (vavg $\approx 0\text{ V}$), but the screen showed it *could* deliver power. This usually means the diodes were blocking the charge during the simulated run because the voltage on $C_p$ never reached the threshold.

    *   Let's consider a **Boost Rectifier**.
    *   The piezo current $I_{piezo} = I_p \sin(\omega t)$.
    *   Let's use a full-bridge rectifier first to get a pulsating DC, then a boost converter? No, that's too many components.
    *   How about a **Synchronous Boost** using the piezo's own capacitance?
    *   Piezo is between $pzp$ and $pzn$.
    *   $pzp$ to $L1$ to $n1$.
    *   $n1$ to $S1$ to $pzn$.
    *   $n1$ to $D1$ to $out$.
    *   $pzn$ to $0$.
    *   When $S1$ is closed, $L1$ charges. When $S1$ is open, $L1$ boosts to $out$.
    *   To do this for both half-cycles, we need a more complex structure.

    *   Another idea: **The "Inductive-SSHI" (i-SSHI)**.
    *   It uses an inductor and a switch to flip the voltage on $C_p$.
    *   $C_p$ charges to $V_{oc}$.
    *   Switch closes $L$ across $C_p$ for $t_{on}$, creating an LC oscillation that flips the voltage to $-V_{oc}$.
    *   Now the total swing is $2 V_{oc}$.
    *   Wait, $2 \times 0.76\text{ V} = 1.52\text{ V}$. Still less than $1.8\text{ V}$.
    *   Am I missing something? Let me re-read the goal. $V_{out,min} = 1.8\text{ V}$.
    *   Is it possible that $I_p$ is the *peak* current? Yes.
    *   Wait, if $V_{oc}$ is $0.76\text{ V}$, and we need $1.8\text{ V}$, we *must* have a boost ratio of at least $1.8 / 0.76 \approx 2.37$.
    *   A simple SSHI only gives a factor of 2.
    *   We need a circuit that can boost the voltage further.

    *   The only way to get $V_{out} > 2 \times V_{oc}$ is a switching converter (Boost).
    *   Let's try a **Synchronous Boost Converter** that works on both half-cycles.
    *   Bridge:
        $D1: pzp \to n1$
        $D2: pzn \to n1$
        $D3: 0 \to pzp$
        $D4: 0 \to pzn$
        Wait, that's just a bridge.
    *   Let's try this:
        Piezo $(pzp, pzn)$ connected to a bridge of switches? No, only 4 switches total.
    *   Let's use a **Half-Bridge Boost**:
        1.  $pzp \to L1 \to n1$
        2.  $n1 \to S1 \to pzn$
        3.  $n1 \to D1 \to out$
        4.  $pzn \to 0$
        This boosts the positive half-cycle.
        To boost the negative half-cycle:
        5.  $pzn \to L2 \to n2$
        6.  $n2 \to S2 \to pzp$
        7.  $n2 \to D2 \to out$
        This is the "Dual-Ended-Boost" topology that was explored but scored `nan`. Let's try to refine it.

    *   Wait, if $pzn$ is connected to $0$ in the first half-circuit, and $pzp$ is connected to $0$ in the second? No, that's not how it works.
    *   Let's try:
        $L1: pzp \to n1$
        $S1: n1 \to 0$, ctrl=G1
        $D1: n1 \to out$
        $L2: pzn \to n2$
        $S2: n2 \to 0$, ctrl=G1
        $D2: n2 \to out$
        $G1: SYNC, edges=both, phase=0, ton=...$
        In this setup:
        - When $S1$ and $S2$ are closed, $L1$ charges from $pzp$ and $L2$ charges from $pzn$.
        - Since $pzp$ and $pzn$ have opposite polarities, one inductor will charge and the other will discharge? No.
        - $V_{pzp} = V_{oc} \sin(\omega t)$, $V_{pzn} = -V_{oc} \sin(\omega t)$.
        - If $S1, S2$ are closed, $L1$ sees $V_{pzp}$ and $L2$ sees $V_{pzn}$.
        - One is positive, one is negative. The one that is negative will just be a path to ground.
        - This is why $S1$ and $S2$ should probably be controlled by *different* SYNCs or different phases.
        - But we only have 2 SYNCs.

    *   Let's refine the Dual Boost:
        $G1: edges=pos, phase=0$ (closes $S1$)
        $G2: edges=neg, phase=0$ (closes $S2$)
        $L1: pzp \to n1, S1: n1 \to 0, D1: n1 \to out$
        $L2: pzn \to n2, S2: n2 \to 0, D2: n2 \to out$
        This looks like a valid boost converter for both half-cycles.

    *   Wait, the piezo is a current source $I_p$ in parallel with $C_p$.
        When $S1$ is closed, the current $I_p \sin(\omega t)$ will flow into $L1$ (and $C_p$).
        The voltage $V_{pzp}$ will be determined by the inductor's current.
        Actually, if $S1$ is closed, the piezo current $I_p$ flows into $L1$ and $C_p$.
        The energy stored in $L1$ is $\frac{1}{2} L I_{peak}^2$.
        When $S1$ opens, $L1$ discharges into $out$ through $D1$.
        The peak voltage $V_{out}$ will be $L \frac{di}{dt} \approx L \frac{I_{peak}}{t_{off}}$. This can easily reach $1.8\text{ V}$ or more.

    *   Component count:
        $L1, S1, D1$ (3)
        $L2, S2, D2$ (3)
        $G1, G2$ (2)
        $C1, DZ1$ (2)
        Total = 10 components. Well within the 16 limit.

    *   $G1: edges=pos, phase=0$ (for positive half-cycle)
    *   $G2: edges=neg, phase=0$ (for negative half-cycle)
    *   $S1$ closed during the positive half-cycle. $S2$ closed during the negative.
    *   Wait, the "zero crossing of the piezo current" is where the voltage peaks.
    *   $I(t) = I_p \sin(\omega t)$.
    *   $V(t) = \int \frac{I}{C} dt = -\frac{I_p}{\omega C_p} \cos(\omega t)$.
    *   $I=0$ at $t=0, \pi/\omega$. $V$ is at peak at $t=0, \pi/\omega$.
    *   The SYNC closes switches "at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero crossings of the piezo current".
    *   So $G1$ (pos) and $G2$ (neg) will fire at the peaks.
    *   If we close the switch $S1$ at the positive peak and keep it closed for $t_{on}$, we capture the energy.
    *   Wait, a boost converter typically closes the switch to *build up* current in the inductor, then opens it to *push* that current to the output.
    *   If we close $S1$ at the peak, we are just shorting the piezo.
    *   We should close $S1$ *before* the peak to build current.
    *   Actually, the simplest way to use a SYNC is to have it closed for a short $t_{on}$ at the peak.
    *   Let's reconsider:
        The energy is stored in $C_p$. At the peak, the voltage is $V_{oc}$.
        If we close $S1$ (connecting $n1$ to $0$), the current from $C_p$ flows into $L1$.
        This is exactly what SSHI does.
        But we want a boost.
        Let's try:
        $pzp \to L1 \to n1$
        $n1 \to S1 \to 0$
        $n1 \to D1 \to out$
        If $S1$ is closed, $L1$ charges from $pzp$.
        If $S1$ is open, $L1$ discharges to $out$.
        To maximize energy, we should close $S1$ when $pzp$ is positive and $S2$ when $pzn$ is positive.
        The SYNC controller fires at the peaks. If $t_{on}$ is small, $S1$ will be closed for a short time around the peak.
        This will charge $L1$ from $C_p$ (and the source $I_p$).
        Then $L1$ will dump the charge into $out$.

    *   Is there a simpler way? What about a **Charge Pump**?
        No, we have inductors. Inductors are better for boosting.
    *   Let's try the **Dual-Ended Boost** again, but with more care about the SYNC settings.
        $G1: edges=pos, phase=0, ton=...$
        $G2: edges=neg, phase=0, ton=...$
        $S1$ controlled by $G1$, $S2$ by $G2$.
        $L1: pzp \to n1, S1: n1 \to 0, D1: n1 \to out$
        $L2: pzn \to n2, S2: n2 \to 0, D2: n2 \to out$

    *   Wait, $L1$ is between $pzp$ and $n1$. If $S1$ is closed, $n1$ is $0$, so $L1$ is across $pzp$ and $0$.
        Current $I_{L1} = \frac{1}{L1} \int V_{pzp} dt$.
        Since $V_{pzp} \approx V_{oc} \sin(\omega t)$, $I_{L1}$ will be $\approx -\frac{V_{oc}}{L1 \omega} \cos(\omega t)$.
        The current in $L1$ will be maximum when $V_{pzp}$ is zero.
        But the SYNC fires at the *peaks* of $V_{pzp}$.
        If $S1$ is closed only at the peak for a very short $t_{on}$, it's like a pulse.
        $I_{L1,peak} \approx \frac{V_{oc} \cdot t_{on}}{L1}$.
        Then this current is pushed through $D1$ to $out$.
